title: Broken by Roles, Restored by Mutation: Mirror Spectra and Equivariant Bifurcations in Role-Conditioned Replicator-Mutator Dynamics
content: A symmetric game acquires an asymmetry as soon as its players can condition their behaviour on an observable but payoff-irrelevant role, such as owner and intruder. Selten's theorem states that no mixed strategy survives as an evolutionarily stable strategy under such role conditioning. We study the dynamical counterpart of this result in the presence of uniform mutation, modelling the two roles as two populations governed by the replicator-mutator dynamic. The system is equivariant under the role swap, its fixed-point subspace carries the role-blind dynamic, and at every symmetric rest point the Jacobian splits into a role-blind block and a transverse block. Without mutation the two spectra are exact mirror images, so the rate at which a symmetric equilibrium attracts in the role-blind game is precisely the rate at which it repels once roles are observed. Mutation shifts both spectra by the same amount. For games whose barycentre is a rest point we prove that the role-conditioned equilibrium is asymptotically stable if and only if the mutation rate exceeds the largest modulus of the real parts of the role-blind spectrum, which for an evolutionarily stable strategy equals its fastest attraction rate. For two-strategy games we obtain closed forms for the threshold, for the critical point, and for the supercritical pitchfork law governing the emerging role conventions, together with a Dulac argument that excludes cycles. For three or more strategies the symmetry-breaking mode can be complex, and an equivariant Hopf bifurcation produces anti-phase role cycles in which the two roles follow the same orbit half a period apart, as we verify for the rock-paper-scissors game. Forced symmetry breaking and finite-population simulations complete the analysis. The results read the emergence of property-like conventions as spontaneous symmetry breaking controlled by the exploration rate.
